newsitem.title: USA: Home prices edge higher as lumber soars.
newsitem.headline: Home prices edge higher as lumber soars.

text.p: Home prices are edging higher as builders pay record prices for lumber, and tight supplies of key grades like spruce lumber should keep prices firm next year.
"In the last three months we have probably added $600 to $700 per house," said Steve George, vice president of Cambridge Homes, a Chicago-area home-building firm.
Home prices should continue rising as record high lumber prices are passed on to home buyers in coming months, industry sources said.
Lumber prices have risen this year due to increased demand for housing and restrictive quotas on the amount of spruce arriving from Canada. The quotas were effective April 1.
Spruce lumber, a key species used for wall studs, jumped to a record $480 per thousand board feet last week from $426 the previous week, according to Random Lengths, a lumber industry newsletter.
The National Home Builders Association said the one-week increase would translate into about an $800 rise in the cost of a $150,000 home.
Lumber industry analysts estimate the nearly year-long rise in lumber prices has already added an average of $4,000 to the price of a home, versus a year ago.
Spruce prices are up 40 percent in the last six months, according to Random Lengths.
If lumber prices continue to rise, as some analysts believe, Cambridge Homes may consider replacing wood wall studs with steel ones, George said.
"I'll be nervous if the spike this past week lasts six weeks," said Art Titus, president of Sundance Homes in Schaumburg, Ill., another Chicago suburb.

Titus said prices for Sundance-built homes, which range from $90,000 to $450,000, have risen 3 to 4 percent this year. Although spruce prices have skyrocketed, he said prices for other building components have not, limiting material cost increases to 2 to 3 percent.

Last week's price spike was triggered by the Canadian government assigning quotas to individual Canadian mills after Canadian shipments surpassed July-September national quotas by 155 million board feet. Those shipments were slapped with export fees, based on the United States-Canada agreement.
The United States produces a small amount of spruce but not enough to meet demand, and southern pine wood, which is plentiful here, is a secondary choice of builders.
"U.S. (spruce) producers cannot handle the demand in the U.S., it is not possible," said Roger Champagne, a wholesale lumber dealer with Capital Forest Products Inc., in Wayne, Pa.

Under the U.S.-Canadian agreement, Canadian mills can ship without penalty 14.7 billion board feet of lumber into the United States annually. Each Canadian lumber mill was assigned a shipment quota. If a mill exceeds its quota, a fine of $50 for every thousand board feet over the quota will be assessed. The fine increases to $100 if shipments exceed a secondary quota level.
Some Canadian lumber mills have been willing to absorb the penalties, hoping to recoup the money through higher lumber prices in the United States.

"My information is there are 50 to 60 mills in Quebec that have already exceeded their quotas ... and are already in the penalty phase," said Curt Cunningham, a lumber analyst and president of Pacific Futures Trading Co.
As a result, Cunningham expects spruce prices to continue climbing as the penalties are passed on to consumers.
"I have a market target of $520 to $530" per thousand board feet, Cunnigham said.
In addition to the Canadian situation, he said demand from home builders has been strong, with home building rates the highest in a decade.
"We have had remarkable home sales this year," he said.
